questions.q: What is noise, as the summary defines it?
a: A random error in our judgment
A deliberate bias we choose
A lack of information
A conflict between experts
questions.why: The overview defines noise as a random mistake in judgment, made without realizing it.

a: Favoring information that supports a desired outcome
Reaching a decision too slowly
Ignoring the most recent evidence
Trusting experts over your own view
questions.why: Lesson 1 says we sometimes want a result so much that we read all information in its favor.

questions.q: Why can simple algorithms outperform experienced judges?
a: Noise and emotion blur human judgment
Algorithms have more information
Judges are not trained in law
Algorithms never make mistakes
questions.why: Lesson 2 says noise blurs judgment and lets emotion disturb rationality, so basic formulas can do better.

a: Independent opinions whose noise cancels out
A crowd that shares the same bias
One expert guiding the group
Averaging only the highest estimates
questions.why: Lesson 3 says averaging varied, independent answers cancels noise and lands close to the truth.

questions.q: What condition must a crowd meet for averaging to help?
a: Members must be independent and diverse
Members must agree before answering
Members must be experts in the field
Members must answer as a group
questions.why: Lesson 3 says opinions must be independent, the question identical, and the crowd diverse in its biases.
